posts.title: What to Post When You Have No Ideas: 5 Quick Fixes
posts.description: Stuck on what to post? 5 quick fixes for creative block: answer a question, react to something, share one small lesson, and film in 60 seconds.
posts.body:
You open your phone, you want to post, and your head is empty. This is normal. It is not a talent problem. "Come up with something" is just a hard job, because it is so open. These five fixes make the job smaller.

## 1. Answer a question instead of inventing a topic

"What should I post?" is too open. A question is easier. Pick one and answer it for 30 seconds:

- What is a small thing that made your day better this week?
- What is something you changed your mind about?
- What is the worst advice you ever got?

Someone asks, you answer. No planning needed.

## 2. React to something

Reacting is easier than creating. Watch a short video, read a comment, or look at a headline. Then say what you think in one or two sentences. Your opinion and your face are enough to make a video.

## 3. Share one small lesson from today

You do not need to be an expert. What did you learn this week? How did you fix a small problem? "I tried this, here is what happened" is a complete video.

## 4. Use a Would You Rather or a light hot take

Two options make it easy to talk. "Would you rather have free coffee forever or free parking forever? Why?" Friendly hot takes about food, habits and daily life start comments, because everyone has an opinion.

## 5. Lower the bar: film 60 seconds, then decide

Press record, answer, and watch it back. You are allowed to delete it. This takes the pressure off, because filming and posting become two separate decisions.

## A shortcut for fixes 1 and 4

KipFire is a free iPhone app that gives you a prompt card, like a funny question, a Would You Rather or a Hot Take. You react on camera, and the card stays in the video, so viewers know what you are answering. It skips the blank page. You can also do the same thing with a list of questions in your notes app.

## Keep it small

One short video a day, or a few a week, is enough. Showing up beats being perfect.

For more ready ideas, see [30 prompts for Reels and TikTok](/tips/what-to-post-on-reels/). If you freeze when you press record, try [15 easy openers for what to say on camera](/tips/what-to-say-on-camera/).

posts.title: Why Real Faces Still Win as AI Videos Fill Your Feed
posts.description: AI videos are everywhere, but a real face and voice still build trust. Learn what only you can offer and simple steps to show your face, even if you're shy.
posts.body:
Scroll for a minute and you will probably see a video that no camera ever filmed. AI tools can now make a realistic person, a voice and a whole scene from a few lines of text. Some of it is impressive. Some of it is hard to tell apart from the real thing.

So you might be asking: if a computer can make a perfect video in seconds, why would anyone want to watch my shaky, nervous one?

Here is the honest answer. As AI videos get more common, a real human face becomes more valuable, not less. This guide explains why, what people can't get from AI content, and how to start showing your face even if the camera scares you.

## Why a real face builds trust

People have been reading faces their whole lives. We notice a small smile, a pause, a nervous laugh, eyes that look away before an honest answer. Those tiny signals tell us that someone is real and means what they say.

A polished AI video can copy how a face looks. What it can't do is stand behind its words. When you speak on camera, there is a real person who will still hold that opinion tomorrow, who will answer comments, and who lived the story they're telling. Viewers feel that difference, even when they can't explain it.

That's also why platforms are adding labels. When YouTube introduced its disclosure tool for realistic altered or synthetic content, it said that ["viewers increasingly want more transparency about whether the content they're seeing is altered or synthetic"](https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/disclosing-ai-generated-content/). People want to know what's real. A real face, filmed by you, answers that question before anyone has to ask.

## What audiences can't get from AI content

AI can make a video about almost anything. But it can't make a video about you. There are three things only you can bring.

- **Your opinion.** An AI can list both sides of "pineapple on pizza". It can't actually care. When you say "honestly, I'd pick the beach every time, and here's why", that's a real position from a real person. People follow people whose opinions they enjoy, agree with or love to argue with.
- **Your reactions.** The moment you hear a weird question and your face does something before you've even answered. The laugh you didn't plan. The "wait, what?" look. Reactions can't be faked well, and they are often the best part of a video.
- **Your story.** Your bad first job, the hike where you complained the whole time, the thing that happened at the store this morning. Nobody else has those memories. A short real story is something no tool can generate for you, because it never happened to the tool.

Put simply: AI is good at information. You are good at being a person. Those are different jobs, and the second one is what makes people come back.

## You don't need to be perfect. That's the point.

A lot of beginners think they have to look and sound like a professional before they post. As AI makes flawless video easy, the opposite is true. Small imperfections are proof that you're real.

A stumble over a word, a laugh in the middle of a sentence, messy hair, a plain wall behind you: none of these ruin a video. They make it feel like a conversation with a real person instead of an ad.

That doesn't mean "low effort". Good light from a window and clear sound still help. But you don't need a perfect script, a perfect face or a perfect room. You need to be honest and to press record.

## Practical steps to show your face, even if you're shy

If filming yourself feels scary, don't try to go from zero to a five-minute talking video. Build up in small, safe steps.

**1. Start smaller than you think**

Your first video doesn't need to be posted. Record a 15-second clip just for yourself and delete it. Then do it again tomorrow. The goal is to get used to the red dot, not to make something great. If you want a full plan for this stage, read [How to Stop Being Scared of the Camera](/tips/how-to-stop-being-scared-of-the-camera/).

**2. React to a prompt instead of inventing a topic**

The hardest part of filming is often not the camera. It's the empty moment when you have no idea what to say. Skip that by giving yourself a question first: a would-you-rather, a hot take, a "what's something that instantly makes your day better?"

Now you're not "making content". You're just answering. Use a simple order: say your answer, give one reason, add one small real moment. For ready-made first lines and examples, see [What to Say on Camera When Your Mind Goes Blank](/tips/what-to-say-on-camera/).

This is exactly why we built **KipFire**: you pick a prompt card (Funny, Challenges, Questions, Would You Rather, Hot Take, Inner Me or For You) and react to it on camera. The card stays in the video, so viewers see the question and your real reaction to it.

**3. Keep it short**

Twenty honest seconds beat three minutes you're too scared to post. Short videos are easier to film, easier to watch and much easier to finish. You can always make longer ones later.

**4. Let the first take be good enough**

Your first take usually sounds the most natural. If you film the same thing ten times, you start to sound like you're reading. Unless you made a real mistake, keep the first or second take and move on.

**5. Show a little more each time**

If a full face feels like too much, start with your voice over your hands, or a side angle. Next week, look at the lens for one sentence. The week after, try a whole answer. Each step only has to be a little braver than the last.

## A simple weekly routine

Consistency matters more than any single video. Here is an easy routine that fits around school, work or a busy week:

- **Monday:** Answer one funny or easy question. Keep it under 30 seconds.
- **Wednesday:** Share one opinion or hot take, with one reason why.
- **Friday:** Tell one small story from your week.
- **Weekend:** Watch your three clips back. Notice one thing you did better than last week. Post the one you like most, or none at all.

That's three short videos a week, and none of them need a script. After a few weeks, you'll have dozens of reps, and pressing record will feel far less dramatic.

## The bottom line

AI will keep getting better at making videos. It will never get better at being you. Your opinions, your reactions and your stories are the one thing a tool can't copy, and in a feed full of generated content, that's exactly what makes people stop scrolling.

You don't need to be confident first. You need one small, real video today. If you want a question to start with, [get KipFire on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kipfire/id6755289956), pick a card and show your face for 20 seconds.

posts.title: What to Say on Camera When Your Mind Goes Blank: 15 Easy Openers
posts.description: Freeze the moment you hit record? Use these 15 simple first lines, a 3-part speaking formula, and real examples to talk on camera without a script.
posts.body:
You press record. The red dot is on. And suddenly your brain is empty.

If that happens to you, you are not bad at this. Lots of people freeze in the first few seconds. The problem is not you. The problem is that you started with nothing to react to.

This guide fixes that. You will get 15 first lines you can use today, a simple 3-part formula for what to say next, and a few tricks that make talking to a camera feel normal.

## Why your mind goes blank

When you talk to a friend, they ask you something and you answer. Your brain is great at answering. It is bad at starting from zero.

A camera does not ask you anything. So you sit there trying to invent a topic, a first line and a point, all at once. That is three hard jobs in one second.

The fix is simple: **give yourself a question first.** Then you are not "making content". You are just answering.

## 15 first lines that always work

Pick one, say it out loud, and keep talking.

- "Okay, honest answer..."
- "Nobody asked, but here's what I think."
- "I got this question today and I actually don't know..."
- "This is going to sound weird, but..."
- "Rate my day so far. Out of ten, it's a..."
- "Unpopular opinion:"
- "Something happened today that I can't stop thinking about."
- "If I'm being honest with myself..."
- "Let me tell you the worst advice I ever followed."
- "Quick question for you, then my answer."
- "I tried something today for the first time."
- "Would you rather... okay, I'll go first."
- "Day one of trying this. Don't judge me."
- "Three things I learned this week. Number one..."
- "I have a confession."

Notice something? Most of them are reactions. They start in the middle of a thought, like you are already in a conversation.

## The 3-part formula: Answer, Why, Story

After your first line, you only need three things:

- **Answer.** Say your answer in one sentence. "I'd pick the beach."
- **Why.** Give one reason. "Because the mountains make me tired just thinking about them."
- **Story.** Add one small real moment. "Last summer I hiked for six hours and complained the whole time."

That's it. That's a full video. Usually 20 to 40 seconds.

Here is a full example. The question is: "What's a tiny thing that instantly makes your day better?"

"Okay, honest answer: a green light when I'm already late. Because it feels like the universe is on my side for two seconds. This morning I hit four in a row and I felt like a main character."

No script. No planning. Just answer, why, story.

## Tricks that make talking to a camera easier

- **Look at the lens, not your face.** Your own face on screen distracts you. Some people put a small sticker next to the lens.
- **Talk to one person.** Imagine one friend watching, not "the internet".
- **Keep the first take.** Your first take often sounds the most natural. Don't film it twelve times.
- **Start the recording before you're ready.** Cut the first two seconds later. Waiting to feel ready is what makes you freeze.
- **Keep it short.** A 20-second honest answer beats a 3-minute speech you're scared to post.

## Where to get questions every day

The hardest part is still finding a good question each day. A few easy sources:

- Questions your friends or followers ask you.
- Comments under other creators' videos.
- "Would you rather" lists and hot take prompts.
- Your own day: what you ate, where you went, what annoyed you.

If you want questions ready on your phone, **KipFire** gives you a prompt card (funny questions, challenges, would you rather, hot takes and more) and you react to it on camera. The card stays in the video, so viewers see the question you're answering. That's the whole idea: you didn't have to invent the topic, you're just reacting.

## The real goal

You don't need to become a confident speaker overnight. You just need to answer one question today. Then another tomorrow.

After a week of small answers, the red dot stops feeling scary. That's how momentum starts.

[Get your first card on KipFire](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kipfire/id6755289956) and say your first line today.

posts.title: How to Stop Being Scared of the Camera: 10 Small Steps
posts.description: Scared to film yourself? Start small: record audio only, film without posting, use a prompt so you don't need ideas, and post a 15-second video first.
posts.body:
You stop being scared of the camera by doing small, safe reps, not by waiting until you feel confident. Start with steps that can't go wrong: record your voice only, film videos you never post, and use a prompt so you don't have to invent what to say. Confidence comes after the reps, not before.

Below are 10 small steps. You don't need all of them. Pick the one that feels a little uncomfortable, but not scary, and start there.

## Why am I so scared of the camera?

Camera fear is normal. When the red light turns on, your brain feels watched and judged, even if nobody is in the room. Most people are not scared of the camera itself. They are scared of three things:

- **Looking silly.** "What if I look awkward or sound weird?"
- **Not knowing what to say.** The blank moment after you press record.
- **Other people seeing it.** Friends, family, coworkers, strangers in the comments.

Each step below takes away one of these fears. Some remove the "what to say" problem. Some remove the "people will see it" problem. Some just get you used to your own face and voice.

I know this fear well. For years I wanted to make content and couldn't talk to the camera. When I finally started, I tried to make every video perfect and burned out in two weeks. That's why I built KipFire. You can read the full story on my [founder page](/founder/).

## What is the easiest way to start if I'm terrified?

Start without your face. These first steps feel almost too easy. That's the point.

**1. Record audio only.** Open your voice memo app and talk for 30 seconds. Answer something simple: "What did I eat today and was it good?" Listen back once. Most people hate their recorded voice at first. After five or six recordings, it starts to sound like you.

**2. Film without posting.** Turn on the front camera and record a 20-second clip. Then delete it. Do this every day for a week. You are not making content yet. You are teaching your brain that the red light is not dangerous.

**3. Delete freely.** Give yourself permission to delete everything. Nothing you film has to exist tomorrow. When you know you can delete it, you stop performing and start talking normally.

## How do I know what to say on camera?

The blank moment after you press record is where most people freeze. The fix is simple: never start from zero.

**4. Use a prompt so you don't need ideas.** A prompt is one short question or statement you react to. "Would you rather never use social media again or never watch a movie again?" You don't need a script. You just answer. Answering a question is much easier than "presenting" something.

This is why prompt-card videos work so well for beginners. The prompt is your first line, and viewers see what you're reacting to. If you want to know more about this format, read [what prompt-card videos are](/tips/what-are-prompt-card-videos/).

**5. Talk to one person, not an audience.** Look at the lens and picture one friend. Talk like you're sending them a voice note. "Hey, so here's my answer..." One friend is easy. "Everyone on the internet" is not.

**6. Write three bullet points, not a script.** If you want some structure, write three short words on a sticky note next to your phone. Reading a full script makes you sound stiff. Three bullet points keep you on track and still sound natural.

## How do I stop feeling awkward watching myself?

Watching yourself back is often harder than filming. A few rules help.

- **Watch once.** Not ten times. Every replay makes you find a new "flaw" nobody else would notice.
- **Look at the message, not your face.** Ask "Did I answer the question?" instead of "Do I look okay?"
- **Keep the imperfect take.** Small pauses and "hmm" make you sound real. Perfect delivery often sounds fake.

**7. Be a little goofy on purpose.** On your first takes, make a silly face, mess up a word on purpose, laugh at yourself. Once you've already "failed" on purpose, the pressure is gone.

## When should I post my first video?

Post sooner than you think, but make it tiny.

**8. Make your first post 15 seconds.** Not a full introduction, not a 3-minute story. One question, one answer, 15 seconds. A short video is easier to film, easier to watch, and much less scary to post.

**9. Post where it feels safest first.** If posting on your main account feels too scary, start with a new account no friends follow, or share it to a close friends list first. Early videos usually get few views. That's not a failure. It's a quiet place to practice.

**10. Repeat for 7 days.** One short video a day for a week. Don't judge anything before the end of the week. The second video is almost always easier than the first, and by day seven, most of the fear is about the first second, not the whole video.

## What does a simple 7-day plan look like?

If you like a plan, try this:

- **Day 1:** Record a 30-second voice memo. Listen once.
- **Day 2:** Film a 20-second video. Delete it.
- **Day 3:** Film yourself answering one question. Keep it, don't post.
- **Day 4:** Film three short takes of the same answer. Keep the most natural one.
- **Day 5:** Post a 15-second answer to one prompt.
- **Day 6:** Post a "would you rather" or a hot take.
- **Day 7:** Post one more and look back at day 1. Notice how much easier it got.

If you want more ideas for what to film after the first week, read [how to start making content on camera](/tips/how-to-start-making-content-on-camera/).

## Do I need special equipment?

No. Your phone is enough. Stand or sit facing a window for light. Find a quiet room. Hold the phone at eye level, or lean it against a few books. That's it. Buying a ring light or a microphone before you've posted anything is often just a way to delay starting.

## Can a prompt app help?

If the hardest part for you is "I don't know what to say," a prompt app removes that step. In KipFire you pick a card category (Funny, Challenges, Questions, Would You Rather, Hot Take, Inner Me, or For You), get a short card, and react on camera. The card text stays in the video, so you don't need to explain the setup. Videos save to your phone first, so you can film without posting and delete anything you don't like.

It's free to start: 5 cards a day without an account, 10 with one.

## FAQ

**Is it normal to be scared of the camera?**
Yes. Most people feel nervous the first time they film themselves. It usually gets easier with short, regular practice, not with waiting.

**How long does it take to get comfortable on camera?**
It's different for everyone. Many people notice a change after a week of small daily videos. The goal is not zero nerves. It's being able to press record even when you feel a little nervous.

**Should I start faceless?**
You can. Voice-only or hands-only videos are a fine first step. When you're ready, try one short face video a week, like answering a single question.

**What should my first video be about?**
Something you can answer without thinking: a question about you, a would-you-rather, or a small opinion. Keep it 15 seconds.

**What if people I know see it?**
Start with an account they don't follow, or post a very short, simple video first. Most people are far less focused on your videos than you fear.

Ready to try your first card? [Get KipFire on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kipfire/id6755289956). It's free for iPhone and iPad.

posts.title: What Are Prompt Card Videos? How to Make One Today
posts.description: Prompt card videos let you film without a script: pick a card, answer it on camera, post. Here is how they work, 15 card ideas and easy steps to start.
posts.body:
What is a prompt card challenge video?

A prompt card challenge video is a short clip where you get a question or a task on a card and react to it on camera. The card stays on screen, so viewers read the same prompt you are answering. Then they think about their own answer, and many want to try it too.

You have probably seen versions of this already: anonymous question stickers, "Add Yours" chains, conversation card games filmed with friends. The idea is always the same. **Someone else gives you the prompt, and you just answer it.**

## Why this format works so well for beginners

The hardest part of making content is often not the camera. It is the blank page. A card removes that problem.

- **You do not need an idea.** The card is the idea.
- **You do not need a script.** You answer like you would answer a friend.
- **It feels less awkward.** You are not "performing", you are responding to a task.
- **Viewers get it in one second.** They read the card and know exactly what the video is about.
- **It invites replies.** People love to comment with their own answer.

## 15 prompt card ideas to try

Here are simple prompts you can film today. Pick one that gives you a real reaction.

**Questions**
- What is a small thing that makes your day better?
- What did you believe as a kid that turned out to be wrong?
- What is the best advice you ignored?

**Would you rather**
- Would you rather know every language or play every instrument?
- Would you rather always be 10 minutes late or always 30 minutes early?
- Would you rather live without music or without movies?

**Hot takes**
- A popular food you think is overrated.
- A habit everyone recommends that does not work for you.
- An "old" thing that was better than the new version.

**Challenges**
- Explain your job in 10 seconds.
- Say three things you are grateful for without pausing.
- Describe your week using only one word, then explain it.

**Inner me**
- Something you are proud of that nobody knows about.
- What would you tell yourself one year ago?
- What are you working on becoming?

## How to make your first prompt card video

**1. Pick the card first, then press record.** Do not plan your answer for an hour. Your first honest reaction is usually the best part.

**2. Keep the card visible.** If viewers cannot read the prompt, the video loses its meaning. Put it near the top of the screen, away from captions and buttons.

**3. Start talking in the first second.** Read the card out loud or jump straight into your answer. No "hi guys, so today...".

**4. Give one clear answer and one reason.** For example: "Hot take: breakfast is overrated. I think better when I eat later." That is already a full video.

**5. End with a question.** Ask viewers what they would answer. This turns your video into a conversation.

**6. Keep it short.** 15 to 40 seconds is enough for most prompts.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Overthinking the answer.** A prompt video should feel spontaneous.
- **Hiding the card.** The card is what makes people stop scrolling.
- **Picking prompts you do not care about.** If you feel nothing, the viewer feels nothing.
- **Waiting for a perfect setup.** A phone, window light and a quiet room are enough.

## Why real faces matter more now

There is more and more AI-generated content online. A real person giving an honest, unplanned answer stands out. Prompt card videos are built for exactly that: a real face, a real reaction, no script.

## Make it a habit

The easiest way to post often is to remove decisions. One card a day is a simple system: open, pick, answer, post. That is how you **keep fire**, meaning you keep your momentum going.

If you want a ready deck of prompts, **KipFire** gives you cards in categories like Funny, Challenges, Questions, Would You Rather, Hot Take and Inner Me. You pick a card, film your reaction, and the card stays in your video. [Download KipFire on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kipfire/id6755289956).

posts.title: 100 Would You Rather Questions for Videos
posts.description: 100 clean Would You Rather questions to film for Reels, TikTok and Shorts, plus 3 tips to make viewers answer in the comments.
posts.body:
Would You Rather questions are one of the easiest video formats. They are short, everyone has an opinion, and viewers answer in the comments. Here are 100 questions you can film today. They are clean and friendly, so they work for any audience.

## How to film a Would You Rather video

**1. Answer fast.** Show the question as text on screen and say your choice in the first two seconds. Then explain why in one or two sentences.

**2. Ask the viewer.** End with "What would you pick?" People love to disagree, and comments help the video reach more people.

**3. Make it a series.** Post one question a day, or answer five in one video. Ask a friend or your partner to answer too, and compare.

## Everyday life

- Would you rather never use an alarm again or never be late again?
- Would you rather always be 10 minutes early or always be 10 minutes late?
- Would you rather give up your phone for a week or give up coffee for a month?
- Would you rather have a perfectly clean room forever or a perfectly organized phone forever?
- Would you rather wake up at 5 a.m. every day or go to bed at 3 a.m. every day?
- Would you rather never wait in line again or never sit in traffic again?
- Would you rather lose your voice for a week or lose your phone for a week?
- Would you rather always know what time it is or always know which way is north?
- Would you rather have no internet for a month or no hot water for a month?
- Would you rather only wear one color forever or only wear one outfit forever?
- Would you rather live without music or without movies?
- Would you rather have every red light turn green or always find a parking spot?
- Would you rather be able to pause time or rewind time by 10 seconds?
- Would you rather never get sick again or never feel tired again?
- Would you rather read minds for one day or be invisible for one day?

## Food

- Would you rather eat pizza every day or never eat pizza again?
- Would you rather give up sweets or give up salty snacks forever?
- Would you rather only eat breakfast food or only eat dinner food?
- Would you rather cook every meal yourself or never be allowed to cook again?
- Would you rather eat the same meal every day or never eat the same meal twice?
- Would you rather always have to eat spicy food or never eat spicy food again?
- Would you rather have unlimited free sushi or unlimited free burgers?
- Would you rather drink only water forever or never drink water again (but stay healthy)?
- Would you rather give up cheese or give up chocolate?
- Would you rather be a famous chef or a famous food critic?
- Would you rather eat dessert first every time or never eat dessert again?
- Would you rather have a personal chef or a personal driver?
- Would you rather only eat cold food or only eat hot food?
- Would you rather eat fries without salt or pizza without cheese?
- Would you rather try every food in the world once or eat your favorite food every day?

## Superpowers and fantasy

- Would you rather fly or teleport?
- Would you rather talk to animals or speak every human language?
- Would you rather be super strong or super fast?
- Would you rather see 10 years into the future or 100 years into the past?
- Would you rather breathe underwater or never need to sleep?
- Would you rather have a rewind button for your life or a pause button?
- Would you rather be the main character in a movie or in a video game?
- Would you rather live in a fantasy world or a sci-fi world?
- Would you rather have a pet dragon or a pet unicorn?
- Would you rather know how you will die or when you will die?
- Would you rather be able to change the past or see the future?
- Would you rather be famous now and forgotten later, or unknown now and famous after you're gone?
- Would you rather have a robot that cleans or a robot that cooks?
- Would you rather meet your future self or your past self?
- Would you rather live 200 years as you are now or 80 years as a superhero?

## Money and work

- Would you rather have $1 million now or $10,000 every month for 10 years?
- Would you rather do a job you love for little money or a boring job for a lot of money?
- Would you rather work 4 long days a week or 6 short days a week?
- Would you rather be your own boss or have a great boss?
- Would you rather work from home forever or in a cool office forever?
- Would you rather retire at 40 with a little money or at 65 with a lot?
- Would you rather be rich and unknown or famous and broke?
- Would you rather win the lottery or have your dream job?
- Would you rather have a long vacation once a year or a long weekend every month?
- Would you rather never pay rent again or never pay for food again?
- Would you rather get paid to travel or get paid to sleep?
- Would you rather start your own business or invest in a friend's business?
- Would you rather be the best in your company or the happiest in your company?
- Would you rather have a 1-minute commute and a small home, or a 1-hour commute and a big home?
- Would you rather give $1,000 to a stranger or get $100 for yourself?

## Travel

- Would you rather visit every country once or live in one country you love forever?
- Would you rather travel by plane only or by train only?
- Would you rather live by the beach or in the mountains?
- Would you rather travel alone or with your best friend?
- Would you rather explore space or the deep ocean?
- Would you rather spend a year in a big city or a year in a small village?
- Would you rather have a free first-class flight or a free 5-star hotel?
- Would you rather plan every detail of a trip or show up with no plan?
- Would you rather never fly again or never ride in a car again?
- Would you rather live where it's always summer or always winter?

## Social media and creators

- Would you rather have 1 million followers or 1,000 true fans?
- Would you rather go viral once or grow slowly every week?
- Would you rather only post videos or only post photos forever?
- Would you rather read every comment on your videos or never read any?
- Would you rather post every day for a year or once a month for a year?
- Would you rather be famous on TikTok or on YouTube?
- Would you rather have a viral video you hate or a video you love that nobody sees?
- Would you rather film everything in one take or edit every video for hours?
- Would you rather lose all your followers or lose all your photos?
- Would you rather never use filters again or never use music in videos again?
- Would you rather have a famous creator follow you or have your video shown on TV?
- Would you rather know exactly when to post or exactly what to post?
- Would you rather delete social media forever or post your screen time every week?
- Would you rather collab with your favorite creator or get a brand deal from your favorite brand?
- Would you rather livestream for 24 hours or post 24 videos in one day?

## Friends, family and feelings

- Would you rather have one best friend or ten good friends?
- Would you rather always say what you think or never say what you think?
- Would you rather relive your best day or skip your worst day?
- Would you rather be the funniest person in the room or the smartest?
- Would you rather forget your birthday or have everyone else forget it?
- Would you rather know what everyone thinks of you or never know?
- Would you rather have a big party for your birthday or a quiet dinner?
- Would you rather give the perfect gift or get the perfect gift?
- Would you rather be able to stop laughing at the wrong moment or stop crying at the wrong moment?
- Would you rather have a friend who is always honest or a friend who is always kind?
- Would you rather go back to school for one day or skip to retirement for one day?
- Would you rather be the oldest sibling or the youngest?
- Would you rather have your life turned into a movie or a book?
- Would you rather know all the answers or always ask the best questions?
- Would you rather say "yes" to everything for a day or "no" to everything for a day?

## Questions people ask

**What are good Would You Rather questions for TikTok?**
The best ones are quick to read, easy to answer in one word, and a little hard to choose. For example: "Would you rather fly or teleport?" or "Would you rather have 1 million followers or 1,000 true fans?"

**How do I film a Would You Rather video?**
Put the question on screen as text, say your answer in the first seconds, explain why in one or two sentences, then ask viewers to pick in the comments.

**Can I use these questions for free?**
Yes. Use any question from this list in your videos. If you want a new question every time, the KipFire app gives you Would You Rather cards to film.

## Get a new question every time

Lists run out. KipFire has a Would You Rather card type: open the app, get a question, react on camera, and post. The question shows on screen, so the video works even with the sound off.

posts.title: How to Start Making Content on Camera: Ideas and What to Say
posts.description: Never filmed yourself? Easy content ideas for beginners, what to say on camera in your first videos, and how to start with just your phone.
posts.body:
Want to start making videos but don't know what to film or what to say? You're not alone. Most beginners don't fail because of talent. They fail because they never start, or they quit after two weeks. This guide keeps it simple.

## How to start content as a beginner

Use only your phone. No camera, lights, or microphone needed. A quiet room and a window for light is enough.

Film one take. Don't edit for hours. Short and real beats long and perfect.

Keep it 15–60 seconds. Short videos are easier to film and easier to watch.

Post 3–5 times a week. Consistency matters more than quality at the start.

Don't wait to feel ready. Your first 10 videos will feel awkward. That's normal, and it's how everyone starts.

## Content ideas for beginners

Answer a question: "What's one thing you'd tell your younger self?"

Share your opinion: "Hot take: something everyone in my city gets wrong."

Would you rather: "Would you rather lose your phone or your wallet for a week?"

Rate your day from 1 to 10 and explain why.

Tell a small story: the funniest or most awkward thing that happened this week.

Do a quick challenge: "Say 5 things you're grateful for in 10 seconds."

Show your daily life: your job, your gym, your morning coffee, with a short thought.

## What to say on camera

If you freeze on camera, use this simple structure:

Hook (first 2 seconds): Say the question or the topic right away. Example: "Would you rather be rich and alone, or broke with real friends?"

Your answer: Say what you really think. Be honest, not perfect.

One reason or story: "Because last year I”¦"

End with a question: "What would you choose? Tell me in the comments."

The easiest trick: don't invent, react. Read a prompt and answer it like you're talking to a friend. Reacting feels natural, so you won't need a script.

## Why talking on camera with your real face is best for beginners

It's the fastest format. No editing, no b-roll, no special skills.

People connect with faces. Viewers follow people they recognize and trust, not just information.

It builds your personal brand. Every video makes your face and voice more familiar.

It stands out from AI content. Feeds are filling up with AI-generated videos. Real faces, real emotions and real reactions are becoming rarer, and that's why they'll be worth more.

It builds confidence. Each video makes the next one easier.

The best time to start showing your face is now, while real human content still stands out.

## A simple tool to help you start

If you never know what to say, try KipFire, a free iPhone app with prompt cards: questions, challenges, would you rather, hot takes and more. Pick a card, react to it on camera, and the card stays in your video so viewers know what you're answering. One minute, and your video is ready.

## Try KipFire

## FAQ

What should I post if I have no ideas? React to a prompt: a question, a would you rather, or a hot take. It's the easiest way to film without planning.

How do I stop being nervous on camera? Film a lot of short videos. Nervousness drops after your first 10-20 videos.

Do I need to edit my videos? No. For beginners, one-take talking videos work great and save hours.
